content: Quinine is a medication used to treat malaria, a disease caused by parasites transmitted through mosquito bites in regions where malaria is prevalent. The parasites invade the body and reside in tissues such as red blood cells or the liver. Quinine works by targeting and killing the malaria parasites within red blood cells. In some cases, an additional medication, such as primaquine, may be required to eliminate parasites residing in other tissues. Both drugs may be necessary to achieve a complete cure and prevent relapse. Quinine belongs to a class of drugs known as antimalarials. Before starting quinine, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, to quinidine, or to mefloquine, or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Quinine may cause dizziness or blurred vision. Alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can exacerbate these effects. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or engaging in activities requiring alertness or clear vision until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. Quinine may cause a condition known as QT prolongation, which affects the heart rhythm. The risk of QT prolongation may increase if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood can also increase this risk. This may occur if you use certain medications (such as diuretics or water pills) or have conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly needed. Discuss the risks, benefits, and treatment options with your doctor. Quinine passes into breast milk, but it is unlikely to harm most nursing infants. Your doctor may test your infant for a specific enzyme deficiency (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, or G6PD) before you breastfeed. Drug interactions can alter how your medications work or increase your risk for serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use (including prescription/nonprescription drugs and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Other medications can affect the removal of quinine from your body, which may impact how quinine works. Similarly, quinine can slow the removal of other medications from your body, potentially affecting their efficacy. Many drugs besides quinine can affect heart rhythm (QT prolongation), including amiodarone, dofetilide, mefloquine, pimozide, procainamide, quinidine, sotalol, and macrolide antibiotics (such as erythromycin), among others. Quinine is very similar to quinidine. This medication may interfere with certain laboratory tests (such as urine tests for catecholamines, protein, or steroids), potentially causing false test results. If someone overdoses on quinine and exhibits serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. Laboratory and/or medical tests (such as G6PD blood levels, vision tests, blood potassium, liver/kidney function, and EKG) may be performed while you are taking this medication. Keep all medical and lab appointments. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is more than 4 hours after the missed dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store quinine at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Quinine may cause side effects such as mild headache, flushing, unusual sweating, nausea, ringing in the ears, decreased hearing, dizziness, blurred vision, and temporary changes in color vision. It may also cause low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), especially during pregnancy. Symptoms of low blood sugar include sudden sweating, shaking, fast heartbeat, hunger, blurred vision, dizziness, or tingling in the hands/feet. If these symptoms occur, increase your blood sugar by consuming a quick source of sugar such as sugar, honey, candy, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. This medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefit to you outweighs the risk of side effects. A very serious allergic reaction to this drug is rare. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. Always read the Medication Guide and, if available, the Patient Information Leaflet provided by your pharmacist before starting quinine and each time you get a refill. Take this medication 2 to 3 hours before or after taking antacids containing aluminum or magnesium. The dosage and length of treatment depend on your medical condition, the country where you were infected, other medications you may be taking for malaria, and your response to treatment. It is crucial to take this medication (and other malaria medications) exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Do not take more or less of this drug than prescribed. Do not skip any doses. Continue taking this medication until the full prescribed amount is finished, even if symptoms disappear after a few days. This medication works best when the amount of drug in your body is kept at a constant level. Take it at evenly spaced intervals. Notify your doctor if you do not start feeling better after 1 to 2 days of starting this medication.
